title: The Tube Mail

facts.claim: The pneumatic post used a pneumatic tube. Native terms were "poste pneumatique" and "Rohrpost"; cards were "petit bleu" or "carte pneumatique". The "pneumatic tube" carried these cards.

paragraphs.narration: Paris decided to build in 1865. During 1866 a trial line ran from the place de la Bourse, in front of the Palais Brongniart, to the Grand-Hôtel on the boulevard des Capucines.

paragraphs.narration: It was then extended to the central telegraph office on the rue de Grenelle. That trial explains why some sources date the Paris network to 1866, and others to 1868.

paragraphs.narration: So both networks began at a stock exchange, and both began inside the telegraph service. They were not built to carry letters. They carried prices and official dispatches.

paragraphs.narration: In 1877, Laurencin gave the plainest picture of how it worked. The tube, he wrote, was "an immense blowpipe." Instead of a ball of clay, it shot out a piston at great speed, followed by one or several boxes of dispatches.

paragraphs.narration: The blowpipe was drawn iron, polished smooth on the inside. Most Paris tubes were 65 millimetres across. The busiest lines had wider tubes, 80 millimetres across.

paragraphs.narration: Something had to supply the breath. At first, the compressed air came from the force of the city's falling water. From 1871, steam engines took over. A picture from 1891 shows them at work, driving compressors and vacuum pumps.

paragraphs.narration: Those trains mostly ran out of sight. Only the first line, in 1866, was laid in a trench. After 1868, the tubes followed the sewers instead.
